title: What infection control training does a dental practice in Australia need?
description: The Dental Board retired its infection control guidelines in 2022. What registered dental practitioners and practices must still do, train and evidence.
shortAnswer: The Dental Board of Australia retired its Guidelines on infection control on 1 July 2022 and no longer prescribes a practice manual. Registered dental practitioners must still prevent or minimize the spread of infection, follow the shared Code of conduct and the blood-borne virus guidelines, maintain infection prevention knowledge through CPD, and comply with state and territory laws. Practices accredited to the Primary and Community Healthcare Standards must also evidence workforce training in standard precautions, hand hygiene and reprocessing.
keyTakeaways: The Dental Board of Australia retired its Guidelines on infection control on 1 July 2022, after a 2021 review and consultation, and replaced them with a fact sheet and a self-reflective tool.
The expectation to practice in a way that prevents or minimizes the spread of infection did not change. The Board takes action under the National Law and the Code of conduct, not under a guideline.

Registered dental practitioners complete 60 hours of CPD over each three-year cycle, at least 48 of them clinically or scientifically based, and the Board says infection prevention and control education can count.
The Board points practitioners to the NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare and AS 5369:2023 for reprocessing, among other national sources.

Where a dental service is accredited to the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care's Primary and Community Healthcare Standards, Actions 3.04, 3.05 and 3.13 expect training records and competency evidence.
jurisdiction: Australia (national, with state and territory laws)
regulator: Dental Board of Australia, with the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra)
appliesTo: Registered dental practitioners in every division of the Dental Board's register
Dental practice owners and managers responsible for practice systems and work health and safety
Team members who are not registered practitioners but handle instruments, clinical waste or patient areas
Dental services seeking accreditation to the National Safety and Quality Primary and Community Healthcare Standards

sections.heading: Does the Dental Board of Australia still have infection control guidelines?

blocks.text: No. The Dental Board of Australia retired its Guidelines on infection control on 1 July 2022. According to the Board's [infection prevention and control page](https://www.dentalboard.gov.au/Codes-Guidelines/Infection-prevention-and-control), it reviewed the guidelines in 2021 and, after consultation, decided to replace them with a fact sheet and a self-reflective tool.

The Board describes the change in two parts. What has not changed is the expectation that practitioners practice safely, in a way that minimizes the spread of infection. What has changed is that the Board "no longer prescribes specific practice guidelines that you must adhere to or keep at your place of practice". Practitioners are instead expected to use professional judgment so that the guidance and processes they follow are evidence-based, safe and relevant to their practice setting.

The Board gives two reasons: a risk-based, less prescriptive approach better reflects its role of regulating individual practitioners rather than writing clinical guidelines, and a fact sheet can be updated faster than a registered guideline. Its regulatory power was never located in the guideline. As the Board puts it, its power to act "comes from the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law".

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects Dental Board of Australia, NHMRC and Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care material as at November 2026. The Board's fact sheet is dated 8 February 2024 and says it will generally be reviewed every three years, so a revised version may appear in 2027. Check the primary sources before relying on any date or figure.

sections.heading: What must a registered dental practitioner do about infection prevention and control?

blocks.text: A registered dental practitioner must meet four professional obligations and any state, territory or federal laws on infection control. The Board's fact sheet, Guidance for registered dental practitioners: Infection prevention and control, lists the professional obligations as adhering to the Code of conduct, following the Guidelines: Registered health practitioners and students in relation to blood-borne viruses, completing ongoing CPD, and holding appropriate professional indemnity insurance for all aspects of practice.

The fact sheet also says practitioners "must maintain your knowledge and skills in infection prevention and control" by staying aware of evidence-based practice resources and emerging issues. That sentence is the closest thing the Board now has to a training requirement, and it attaches to the individual practitioner rather than to the practice.

items: **Code of conduct:** the shared Code of conduct applies to registered practitioners in 12 professions. The fact sheet highlights the parts on acting within the law, maintaining adequate knowledge and skills, applying public health principles including infection prevention and control, and understanding immunization against communicable diseases.

**Blood-borne viruses:** practitioners and students must comply with the Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) national guidelines for healthcare workers living with blood-borne viruses and those who perform exposure prone procedures.

**CPD:** the Continuing professional development registration standard requires at least 60 hours over a three-year cycle, of which 48 must be clinically or scientifically based and up to 12 can be non-scientific.

**State and territory law:** the fact sheet lists public health laws, place of practice licensing or accreditation rules, work health and safety laws, and environmental laws on waste disposal as examples.

blocks.text: The general CPD framework that sits behind the third point is covered in [what CPD Ahpra requires](/regulations/ahpra-cpd-registration-standards). The Board's [registration standards page](https://www.dentalboard.gov.au/Registration-Standards) lists the dental CPD standard's date of effect as 1 December 2015.

sections.heading: Which infection control guidance should a dental practice follow now?

blocks.text: The practice chooses, but the Board expects the choice to be evidence-based and defensible. The fact sheet names national sources that "can help practitioners be informed about accepted infection prevention and control approaches", including the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare, CDNA publications, the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) standards, Australian Standard AS 5369:2023, the Australian Immunisation Handbook and the National Hand Hygiene Initiative.

The [NHMRC guidelines page](https://www.nhmrc.gov.au/about-us/publications/australian-guidelines-prevention-and-control-infection-healthcare-2019) says the guidelines were updated in May 2019 in partnership with the ACSQHC, are maintained on the MAGICapp platform, and receive minor edits in cycles that currently run in February, June and October. NHMRC states that healthcare associated infections can occur in office-based practices, naming dental clinics, and that facilities should apply the recommendations according to their own setting and risk. Because the guidelines change in place, a practice that cites them should record the version date it trained against.

For reprocessing, the ACSQHC's [Primary and Community Healthcare Standards page](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/national-standards/primary-and-community-healthcare-standards) publishes a gap analysis tool for moving from AS/NZS 4815:2006 to AS 5369:2023, and lists the Australian Dental Association's Guidelines for Infection Prevention and Control (Fifth Edition, Amended) as a dental practice resource. The ADA document is professional guidance, not law, but it is the reference many dental teams already train to.

sections.heading: What do the Primary and Community Healthcare Standards require for infection control training?

blocks.text: Dental services accredited to the National Safety and Quality Primary and Community Healthcare Standards must show that their workforce is trained in the infection control processes the standards require. The ACSQHC says these standards apply to primary and community services including those with a focus on oral health. Several actions in the [Clinical Safety Standard](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/national-standards/primary-and-community-healthcare-standards/clinical-safety-standard) list training documents as examples of evidence.

items: **Action 3.01:** the workforce uses the clinical governance system when identifying training requirements for clinical safety. Suggested evidence includes orientation training plans and records.

**Action 3.04:** standard and transmission-based precautions consistent with the current edition of the NHMRC guidelines. Suggested evidence includes training syllabi, attendance records, competency assessments and observation of practice.
**Action 3.05:** a hand hygiene process consistent with the National Hand Hygiene Initiative, supported by access to hand hygiene training.
**Action 3.11:** a risk-based workforce screening and immunization process consistent with the current Australian Immunisation Handbook.
**Action 3.13:** reprocessing consistent with relevant national and international standards and the manufacturer's instructions, with traceability of critical items to the patient procedure.

blocks.text: Public dental services in hospital settings may instead be assessed against the NSQHS Standards, whose training expectations are covered in [what the NSQHS Standards require for workforce training](/regulations/nsqhs-standards-workforce-training).

sections.heading: How should a dental practice map infection control obligations to roles, frequency and evidence?

blocks.text: Map each source of obligation to the roles it touches, a refresh trigger and the evidence a Board investigator or accreditation assessor would ask for. The table below is an original, illustrative mapping built from the Board's fact sheet and the ACSQHC actions above. Where a frequency is not set by the source, the column says so; the practice sets its own interval and records why.

blocks.text: Observed competency is the evidence that separates a training record from proof of safe practice, which is why reprocessing and precautions rows ask for a sign off rather than a completion date. The glossary entry on [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) explains how to structure that sign off, and the guide to [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers retention and retrieval.

sections.heading: What happens if a notification is made about infection control in a dental practice?

blocks.text: Ahpra and the Board can investigate and take regulatory action even though no infection control guideline exists. The fact sheet says that if a notification is made, the Board may ask about the processes and policies the practitioner follows, the sources of information used to guide practice, and how the Board's standards, codes and guidelines are adhered to, and the place of practice may be inspected.

In practice this means a dental practitioner should be able to name the guidance the practice follows, show the version date, and produce records showing that the team was trained to it. A practice that cannot point to any chosen reference is in a weaker position than one that followed the retired guidelines and kept them current. The employer's separate duty to train workers is described in [the WHS Act duty to provide training](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training).

sections.heading: How can the Board's self-reflective tool be used in a training program?

blocks.text: The self-reflective tool can serve as an annual gap analysis for each practitioner and as the starting point for team training. The Board says the tool helps practitioners identify gaps in knowledge, skills, systems and protocols, plan to address them, and discuss infection control with teams, mentors and colleagues in peer-based or CPD settings.

items: Each registered practitioner completes the tool and records gaps as CPD learning goals.
The practice manager aggregates common gaps across the team without identifying individuals.
Shared gaps become the agenda for a team session, with an observed assessment for practical tasks such as instrument reprocessing.
The practice records the guidance version used, attendance, and the assessment outcome for each person.

blocks.text: The Board notes that completing education to improve infection prevention and control practice can count towards CPD, so this cycle can satisfy the individual and practice requirements together. More on healthcare training obligations across settings is on the [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences) page.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: With no Board guideline to point to, a dental practice's defense is a documented choice of references and evidence that each role was trained and assessed against them. Knowledge Foundry records which external guidance each infection control procedure relies on, with its version date, and links the procedure to the roles and observed assessments that depend on it. When NHMRC edits the guidelines or the reprocessing standard changes, the affected procedures and staff are listed for review.

faqs.q: Can a dental practice keep using the retired Dental Board guidelines?
faqs.a: The Board says practice does not necessarily have to change. If the way a practitioner worked under the retired guidelines remains up to date, evidence-based, safe and appropriate to the setting, there is no need to change it. The guidelines themselves are no longer maintained, so the practice should check its processes against current national sources.

faqs.q: Do dental assistants need infection control training?
faqs.a: The Board regulates registered dental practitioners, so its fact sheet does not address team members who are not registered. Their training comes from the practice's own systems, work health and safety duties, state or territory requirements and, for accredited services, the ACSQHC actions that apply to the whole workforce. Registered practitioners also retain personal accountability for care delivered by their team.

faqs.q: Is there a minimum number of infection control CPD hours for dentists?
faqs.a: No separate infection control hour count is set. The CPD registration standard requires 60 hours over three years, with 48 clinically or scientifically based. The Board says infection control courses are readily available and that education to improve infection prevention practice can count towards the total.

faqs.q: Which Australian Standard covers instrument reprocessing in dental practices?
faqs.a: The Board's fact sheet lists Australian Standard AS 5369:2023 among national guidance, and the ACSQHC publishes a gap analysis tool for transitioning from AS/NZS 4815:2006 to AS 5369:2023. Accredited services must also meet Action 3.13 of the Primary and Community Healthcare Standards on reprocessing and traceability.
